beats.say: Everything you think you know about the Medici begins with a document from fourteen twenty seven. A spreadsheet.
Florence was losing a war with Milan, and the city was broke. So it did something no state had ever done.
It counted everything. Sixty thousand households. Every name, every age, every asset, every debt. Even the mules.
They called it the catasto. Volume after volume of pure data, five centuries before the computer.
And the data held a surprise. The richest man in Florence was not a Medici. Palla Strozzi declared one hundred and sixty three thousand florins. The Medici, seventy nine.
But being number one on a tax list makes you exactly one thing. A target.
Strozzi paid the city's biggest tax bills, year after year. Then politics turned. By fourteen thirty four, Cosimo de Medici ran Florence, and Palla Strozzi was banished for life.
And the census itself? The rich learned to hide their wealth, and the numbers rotted. Economists now have a name for that.

visual.text: When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure.

beats.say: Cosimo had declared less, spent quietly, and bought loyalty instead of splendour. Number two on paper. Number one everywhere else.
The richest man on the list died banished and broken. The runner up built a dynasty that ran Florence for three centuries. Data is not destiny.
